screens.title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal
screens.narratorSegment: Scaling describes how a system increases capacity to handle more load. Vertical scaling, or scaling up, means adding more C P U, R A M, or disk to a single machine. It is often simple to implement because you manage fewer nodes and don’t need distributed coordination, but it hits physical limits and increases risk: the single server remains a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, means adding more servers to share the workload. This offers better fault tolerance — when one machine fails, others continue serving — and allows near-unlimited growth by adding more nodes. However, adding servers brings complexity: you must route traffic between nodes, handle distributed state, and keep data consistent. A common misconception is that horizontal scaling always simplifies costs or complexity; in reality it trades single-node simplicity for distributed systems complexity. For example, converting a session-based login to a horizontally scaled cluster requires either sticky sessions or moving session state to a shared store. The core decision is trade-off based: use vertical scaling for quick capacity increases with limited fault tolerance, and horizontal scaling when you need availability and long-term growth.

content.html:
Definition
Vertical vs Horizontal

Vertical scaling adds resources to a single machine; horizontal scaling adds machines to a pool. Each approach changes availability and operational needs.

Vertical (Scale Up)
Simple to manage, limited by hardware, single point of failure.
Horizontal (Scale Out)
Adds fault tolerance and capacity, requires traffic routing and state management.
Key Takeaway

Choose horizontal scaling when you need availability and growth; expect added complexity around state and routing.

Concrete example

Imagine an API that validates tokens. If it’s stateless, you can add identical servers behind a balancer and scale horizontally. If the same API holds in-memory sessions, horizontalizing requires moving those sessions to a shared cache before adding servers.

When to scale up
Short-term bursts, simple setups, single-process apps.
When to scale out
Growth beyond single machine limits, high availability needs.
Misconception
More servers don’t remove the need for consistent state management.

screens.title: What a Load Balancer Does
screens.narratorSegment: A load balancer acts as an intermediary that receives client requests and forwards them to backend servers. Its primary functions are distributing load, failing over around unhealthy backends, and presenting a single endpoint for clients. Distribution prevents any one server from becoming overwhelmed, and health checks let the balancer route traffic away from failing machines. Another important job is preserving necessary request metadata: forwarding headers so backends can see the original host or client IP. A common misconception is that a balancer itself solves all scaling problems; it does not remove the need to design stateless services or to externalize state. Instead, it enables a pool of servers to share work and simplifies client configuration by hiding backend details. For example, when you use a managed balancer or Nginx in front of two app servers, clients call one public address while the balancer decides which backend will process each request. That separation is what lets you add or remove servers without changing client endpoints. What a Load Balancer Does means distribute requests, perform health checks, and provide a stable public endpoint while abstracting backend changes.. In practical terms, the traffic cop that distributes requests and improves availability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Distribute requests, perform health checks, and provide a stable public endpoint while abstracting backend changes.

content.html:
Core Concept
Load Balancer Responsibilities
  • Distribute inbound requests across backends to balance resource use and latency.
  • Detect unhealthy servers via health checks and stop routing to them.
  • Preserve headers and client IP when required for logging or security.
  • Provide a single public endpoint to simplify client configuration.
Key Takeaway

A load balancer enables pooling of servers and graceful handling of failing backends, but does not eliminate state-management requirements.

Example scenario

A public API endpoint receives thousands of requests per second. A load balancer routes these requests across three identical workers and continuously checks each worker’s health. If worker two fails a health check, the balancer stops sending traffic to it, keeping the API available while operations replace the instance.

Common mistake
Assuming adding a balancer removes the need to make services stateless; it only helps route traffic.
Pro tip
Preserve X-Forwarded-For headers so backends can log original client IPs when needed.

screens.title: Balancing Algorithms: Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Balancers use algorithms to pick which backend receives each incoming request. Three common algorithms are Round Robin, Least Connections, and IP Hash. Round Robin cycles requests sequentially through the server list. It is simple and works well when requests are short and servers have similar capacity, but it does not account for current server load. Least Connections routes to the server with the fewest active connections, which better balances long-lived or uneven requests because it considers current usage. IP Hash computes a hash from the client’s IP address to select a server. This provides a form of session affinity: the same client tends to hit the same backend, which can be helpful for stateful services but can produce uneven distribution if some clients are much heavier than others. Interviewers often ask when to choose each method: use Round Robin for uniform short requests, Least Connections for long connections or uneven loads, and IP Hash when you need simple stickiness without external session stores. Always consider a fallback for uneven client distribution with IP Hash. In practical terms, how round robin, least connections, and ip hash decide where to send requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
Algorithm quick reference
Round Robin
Sequentially rotate servers. Best for short, similar requests. Does not inspect server load.
Least Connections
Route to server with fewest active connections. Adapts to long-lived traffic and uneven request costs.
IP Hash
Map client IP to a server for affinity. Useful for sticky sessions but may produce imbalance if some clients dominate traffic.
Example decisions

If you run short HTTP requests from many clients, Round Robin is often fine. If you host WebSocket connections or video streams that persist, Least Connections will reduce overload on busy nodes. If you must keep a client on one server and cannot externalize state quickly, IP Hash gives an inexpensive form of affinity.

Misconception
IP Hash automatically balances load; it only guarantees client placement, not equal load distribution.
Check your understanding
Which algorithm would you pick for long-lived chat connections? (Hint: consider active connections.)

screens.title: Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin
screens.narratorSegment: Round Robin assigns incoming requests in sequence to each server in the pool. Imagine three identical servers: request one goes to server A, request two to B, request three to C, then request four circles back to A. This method is very simple and effective when requests are uniform and servers have similar capacity. However, not all servers are equal; older machines might have less C P U or network bandwidth. Weighted Round Robin extends the idea by assigning a weight to each server so more capable servers receive more requests. A common error is to rely on static weights without monitoring actual performance; workload characteristics can change and weights may need adjustment. Another misconception is that Weighted Round Robin accounts for instantaneous load — it does not track active connections by default. Use Weighted Round Robin when you are confident about relative server capacities and want a deterministic distribution, but combine it with health checks and monitoring to adapt when capacities change. Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin means round robin cycles through servers; weighted variants account for capacity but do not replace real-time load metrics.. In practical terms, how sequential distribution works and how to adapt it for different server capacities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Round Robin sequence
A
B
C
Requests cycle through these servers in order. Weighted Round Robin multiplies entries when a server’s weight is higher so it appears more often in the cycle.
Concrete example

If Server A has double capacity, a weighted cycle might send two requests to A for every one to B and C. This yields a proportional distribution but still ignores active connection counts.

When to use
Simple traffic patterns where capacity differences are known and stable.
Common mistake
Treating weights as a substitute for live load measurement; they are static unless you automate updates.

screens.title: Least Connections and Least Response Time
screens.narratorSegment: Least Connections routes new requests to the server with the fewest active connections. This makes it well-suited to workloads with long-lived connections, such as WebSockets, streaming, or heavy A P I calls, because it adapts to current usage. Least Response Time extends this idea by routing to the server that responds fastest, combining measured latency with connection counts to favor healthy, responsive nodes. These runtime algorithms reduce the chance of one server becoming overloaded if requests vary widely in cost. A misconception is that Least Connections guarantees equal C P U usage; it balances connections, not C P U or memory. It’s possible for a few connections to be very expensive. In practice, you should pair these algorithms with health checks and capacity-aware autoscaling. For example, if one node consistently shows high connection and high latency, add capacity or remove it from rotation rather than only adjusting the balancer algorithm. Least Connections and Least Response Time means least connections adapts to active workload; least response time uses latency to prefer faster nodes, both requiring monitoring to be effective.. In practical terms, algorithms that use runtime signals to balance uneven loads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow
Least Connections & Response Time
  • Least Connections: choose backend with fewest active connections.
  • Least Response Time: prefer the backend with the fastest observed responses.
Scenario

For chat servers with persistent connections, Least Connections prevents one node from taking too many long-lived sessions. For mixed workloads, Least Response Time can avoid routing to nodes that are experiencing transient slowdowns.

Misconception
These algorithms do not remove the need for autoscaling or state management; they help distribute active load but don’t change application state behavior.
Pro tip
Combine runtime algorithms with autoscaling and health checks to respond to sustained load changes.

screens.title: IP Hash and Sticky Sessions
screens.narratorSegment: IP Hash computes a hash of the client’s IP address to deterministically select a backend. This creates implicit session affinity: a client tends to hit the same server across requests. Sticky sessions are a related feature where the balancer explicitly attaches session affinity, often via cookies or mapping tables. These techniques let stateful servers keep a client’s session in-memory without requiring external storage. The trade-off is reduced fault tolerance and uneven load: if one client generates heavy traffic, the server that receives its hashed or sticky traffic will be busy while others are idle. If that server fails, the user’s session is lost unless there is a fallback. A better long-term approach is to externalize state — move session data to a shared store like Redis — which makes servers stateless and fully fungible. Use IP Hash or sticky sessions as an interim pattern when migrating to an external store is not possible immediately, but plan to remove affinity for robust horizontal scaling. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
IP Hash & Sticky Sessions

Deterministic client mapping allows a client to reach the same backend repeatedly, preserving server-local session state without external storage.

When useful
Short-term compatibility with legacy stateful code or during migration.
Downside
Uneven load and single-server session loss if that backend fails.
Concrete migration path

Start with sticky sessions if you must, while you extract state to a shared store like Redis. After externalizing, remove affinity so any server can handle any request and your cluster regains even distribution and higher fault tolerance.

Key Takeaway

Use affinity for compatibility, and externalize state for true horizontal scalability.

screens.title: Stateless vs Stateful Services
screens.narratorSegment: The distinction between stateless and stateful services is fundamental to scaling. A stateless service treats each request independently; all the information needed to process the request is contained in the request itself or in shared services. Stateless services are inherently easy to scale horizontally: any server can handle any request, and instances can be added or removed without disrupting sessions. A stateful service stores client-specific data on the local server, such as an in-memory session. Scaling stateful services horizontally requires either sticky sessions so clients return to the same server, or externalizing state to a shared store. Sticky sessions reduce fault tolerance and create imbalance, while externalizing state removes those limits but adds complexity: you must design a durable, consistent store and handle cache invalidation, performance, and availability of that store. A common misconception is that moving state to a single shared database solves scaling automatically; it can create a new bottleneck if the store itself is not designed to scale or cache efficiently. The right architecture combines stateless application servers with distributed caches or databases tuned for scale. Stateless vs Stateful Services means stateless services enable easy horizontal scaling; stateful services require affinity or external state stores and careful design of the state layer.. In practical terms, how the service type changes scaling approaches and failure modes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
Stateless vs Stateful

Stateless: any server can handle a request. Stateful: some client data lives on a server.

  • Stateless: easy autoscaling and failure recovery.
  • Stateful: needs affinity or external storage for sessions.
Example

A token validation service that reads each request token and checks it against a shared cache is stateless — any instance can validate tokens. A chat server holding open user sessions in memory is stateful and requires affinity or a migration to a shared store before scaling out safely.

Misconception
A central database alone does not make the system scale; the database must itself be scaled and cached appropriately.

screens.title: Externalizing State: Redis and Shared Stores
screens.narratorSegment: Externalizing state means moving session data or other client-specific information out of application memory into a shared store. Common choices include an in-memory cache like Redis or a distributed database. The benefit is that application servers become stateless: they can be added or removed without losing sessions, and any server can process any request. This increases fault tolerance and simplifies load balancing because you don’t need sticky sessions. However, an external store introduces its own operational concerns: high availability, replication, consistency, and network latency. A misconception is assuming externalizing state is free — it requires design for replication, backup, and scaling the store itself. In practice, you start by identifying the minimal session data to move to the store, use TTLs to limit memory, and ensure the store is replicated. For example, moving login sessions to Redis lets two backend servers at 192.168.1.101 and 192.168.1.102 handle the same user interchangeably while the load balancer focuses purely on distribution. In practical terms, turning stateful servers into stateless workers using an external store. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Architecture
Externalizing state

Move session or other per-client data into a shared store so application servers stay stateless and interchangeable.

Steps
  1. Identify session fields needed across requests.
  2. Store them in a shared cache with TTL.
  3. Update app servers to read state from the store.
Operational concerns
Replication, failover, and latency of the shared store must be planned and monitored.
Concrete example

Move user sessions to Redis. With sessions in Redis, the two backends 192.168.1.101 and 192.168.1.102 can both read session state and serve the same user, eliminating the need for sticky routing.

Key Takeaway

Externalizing state enables robust horizontal scaling, but design and operate the store carefully to avoid a new bottleneck.

keyIdea.title: Nginx pattern
keyIdea.text: Define an upstream group of backends and proxy_pass to it; preserve headers so backends see original host and client IP.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Nginx upstream + server block

Starter snippet and final solution are shown below. Use these in nginx.conf or include them from a site file.

# Nginx configuration snippet
# Define the upstream group of backend servers
upstream backend_servers {
    # Add your backend server definitions here
    # Example: server 192.168.1.101:8080;
    # Example: server 192.168.1.102:8080;
    
    # The default load balancing method is Round Robin, so no explicit directive is needed unless you want another algorithm
}

# Define the server block that listens for incoming HTTP requests
server {
    listen 80; # Listen on port 80 for HTTP traffic
    server_name example.com; # Replace with your domain or IP

    location / {
        # Proxy requests to the upstream group
        proxy_pass http://backend_servers;
        
        # Preserve original host header and client IP
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
}
Solution notes

The solution explicitly lists 192.168.1.101:8080 and 192.168.1.102:8080 in upstream. Round Robin is the default. If you needed Least Connections, you could add a least_conn directive inside the upstream block. Testing with repeated curl requests verifies that responses rotate between backends.

Key Takeaway

A minimal Nginx upstream with proxy_pass and header preservation provides a simple, testable Round Robin load balancer for two backends.

screens.title: Testing Load Distribution and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Validating that your load balancer distributes traffic as expected is an essential step. A simple test is to run repeated HTTP requests to the balancer and inspect which backend responds. In local or mock setups you can run two backend servers that return their hostnames, then curl the balancer several times to observe Round Robin behavior. Watch for sticky-session side effects: if you configured IP Hash or sticky cookies, certain clients will repeatedly hit the same backend. That can be useful for legacy applications, but it can also hide load spikes because a heavy client will keep using its assigned server. Another common mistake is not forwarding client IP headers; without X-Forwarded-For, backend logs will only show the balancer IP and you lose visibility into client behavior. Finally, don’t forget health checks: if a backend becomes unhealthy, remove it from rotation and monitor the impact. Testing should include intentionally shutting down a backend to confirm the balancer correctly redirects traffic and that user sessions survive if state is externalized. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts capture the most important ideas to keep in mind. First, Horizontal Scaling means adding machines to increase capacity and fault tolerance, but requires coordination around state and routing. Second, a Load Balancer distributes traffic, performs health checks, and provides a stable client endpoint while preserving headers that backends may need. These three ideas will guide your decisions when designing systems that must scale reliably.

fullNarratorScript:
As your application grows, a single server eventually becomes a bottleneck. In this lesson we’ll focus on horizontal scaling — adding more servers to share traffic — and the load balancers that route requests across that fleet. You will learn what a load balancer does, why round robin, least connections, and IP-hash behave differently, and why stateless services are easier to scale than stateful ones. We’ll also walk through a practical Nginx configuration that uses Round Robin to distribute HTTP traffic to two backends. Understanding these pieces matters because it helps you design systems that remain available when demand grows and that recover gracefully when individual machines fail. For example, making an app stateless and using a shared cache lets multiple servers handle the same user without losing sessions. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to explain the trade-offs between scaling up and scaling out, choose a balancing strategy for simple scenarios, and write a basic Nginx upstream block that proxies traffic to backend servers.

In this chapter you will gain four concrete competencies that designers rely on when systems grow beyond a single machine. First, you will explain why load balancers exist and how they improve availability and distribute work across servers; being able to articulate that benefit helps you pick appropriate architecture patterns. Second, you will describe several common algorithms such as Round Robin, Least Connections, and IP Hash, and know the situations where each yields better outcomes; that knowledge guides how you configure a balancer for stateful or stateless workloads. Third, you will differentiate vertical scaling from horizontal scaling and identify scenarios where adding resources to one server is preferable or when adding more servers is necessary. Fourth, you will understand the differences between scaling stateful and stateless services and how techniques like sticky sessions or externalizing state change your operational requirements. Each objective is framed so you can explain the why, demonstrate the how, and reason about trade-offs when designing a real system.

Beyond concepts, this chapter trains you to perform two practical steps that often appear in interviews and system design tasks. You will be able to select an algorithm and justify it: for example, choosing Least Connections when requests are long-lived or Round Robin when connections are short and uniform. You will also be able to write and reason about a basic Nginx upstream configuration that directs traffic to multiple backends. That includes preserving headers so your application can see client IPs and knowing when to use sticky sessions versus moving state to an external store. These skills matter because interviewers want both conceptual trade-offs and the ability to produce a short, correct configuration for a working prototype. Practice will emphasize explaining trade-offs aloud, showing a small config snippet, and describing how you would test traffic distribution using simulated requests.

Scaling describes how a system increases capacity to handle more load. Vertical scaling, or scaling up, means adding more C P U, R A M, or disk to a single machine. It is often simple to implement because you manage fewer nodes and don’t need distributed coordination, but it hits physical limits and increases risk: the single server remains a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, means adding more servers to share the workload. This offers better fault tolerance — when one machine fails, others continue serving — and allows near-unlimited growth by adding more nodes. However, adding servers brings complexity: you must route traffic between nodes, handle distributed state, and keep data consistent. A common misconception is that horizontal scaling always simplifies costs or complexity; in reality it trades single-node simplicity for distributed systems complexity. For example, converting a session-based login to a horizontally scaled cluster requires either sticky sessions or moving session state to a shared store. The core decision is trade-off based: use vertical scaling for quick capacity increases with limited fault tolerance, and horizontal scaling when you need availability and long-term growth.

A load balancer acts as an intermediary that receives client requests and forwards them to backend servers. Its primary functions are distributing load, failing over around unhealthy backends, and presenting a single endpoint for clients. Distribution prevents any one server from becoming overwhelmed, and health checks let the balancer route traffic away from failing machines. Another important job is preserving necessary request metadata: forwarding headers so backends can see the original host or client IP. A common misconception is that a balancer itself solves all scaling problems; it does not remove the need to design stateless services or to externalize state. Instead, it enables a pool of servers to share work and simplifies client configuration by hiding backend details. For example, when you use a managed balancer or Nginx in front of two app servers, clients call one public address while the balancer decides which backend will process each request. That separation is what lets you add or remove servers without changing client endpoints. What a Load Balancer Does means distribute requests, perform health checks, and provide a stable public endpoint while abstracting backend changes.. In practical terms, the traffic cop that distributes requests and improves availability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Balancers use algorithms to pick which backend receives each incoming request. Three common algorithms are Round Robin, Least Connections, and IP Hash. Round Robin cycles requests sequentially through the server list. It is simple and works well when requests are short and servers have similar capacity, but it does not account for current server load. Least Connections routes to the server with the fewest active connections, which better balances long-lived or uneven requests because it considers current usage. IP Hash computes a hash from the client’s IP address to select a server. This provides a form of session affinity: the same client tends to hit the same backend, which can be helpful for stateful services but can produce uneven distribution if some clients are much heavier than others. Interviewers often ask when to choose each method: use Round Robin for uniform short requests, Least Connections for long connections or uneven loads, and IP Hash when you need simple stickiness without external session stores. Always consider a fallback for uneven client distribution with IP Hash. Balancing Algorithms: Overview means round robin is simple, least connections adapts to load, and ip hash enforces client affinity at the cost of possible imbalance.. In practical terms, how round robin, least connections, and ip hash decide where to send requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Round Robin assigns incoming requests in sequence to each server in the pool. Imagine three identical servers: request one goes to server A, request two to B, request three to C, then request four circles back to A. This method is very simple and effective when requests are uniform and servers have similar capacity. However, not all servers are equal; older machines might have less C P U or network bandwidth. Weighted Round Robin extends the idea by assigning a weight to each server so more capable servers receive more requests. A common error is to rely on static weights without monitoring actual performance; workload characteristics can change and weights may need adjustment. Another misconception is that Weighted Round Robin accounts for instantaneous load — it does not track active connections by default. Use Weighted Round Robin when you are confident about relative server capacities and want a deterministic distribution, but combine it with health checks and monitoring to adapt when capacities change. Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin means round robin cycles through servers; weighted variants account for capacity but do not replace real-time load metrics.. In practical terms, how sequential distribution works and how to adapt it for different server capacities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Least Connections routes new requests to the server with the fewest active connections. This makes it well-suited to workloads with long-lived connections, such as WebSockets, streaming, or heavy A P I calls, because it adapts to current usage. Least Response Time extends this idea by routing to the server that responds fastest, combining measured latency with connection counts to favor healthy, responsive nodes. These runtime algorithms reduce the chance of one server becoming overloaded if requests vary widely in cost. A misconception is that Least Connections guarantees equal C P U usage; it balances connections, not C P U or memory. It’s possible for a few connections to be very expensive. In practice, you should pair these algorithms with health checks and capacity-aware autoscaling. For example, if one node consistently shows high connection and high latency, add capacity or remove it from rotation rather than only adjusting the balancer algorithm. Least Connections and Least Response Time means least connections adapts to active workload; least response time uses latency to prefer faster nodes, both requiring monitoring to be effective.. In practical terms, algorithms that use runtime signals to balance uneven loads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IP Hash computes a hash of the client’s IP address to deterministically select a backend. This creates implicit session affinity: a client tends to hit the same server across requests. Sticky sessions are a related feature where the balancer explicitly attaches session affinity, often via cookies or mapping tables. These techniques let stateful servers keep a client’s session in-memory without requiring external storage. The trade-off is reduced fault tolerance and uneven load: if one client generates heavy traffic, the server that receives its hashed or sticky traffic will be busy while others are idle. If that server fails, the user’s session is lost unless there is a fallback. A better long-term approach is to externalize state — move session data to a shared store like Redis — which makes servers stateless and fully fungible. Use IP Hash or sticky sessions as an interim pattern when migrating to an external store is not possible immediately, but plan to remove affinity for robust horizontal scaling. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The distinction between stateless and stateful services is fundamental to scaling. A stateless service treats each request independently; all the information needed to process the request is contained in the request itself or in shared services. Stateless services are inherently easy to scale horizontally: any server can handle any request, and instances can be added or removed without disrupting sessions. A stateful service stores client-specific data on the local server, such as an in-memory session. Scaling stateful services horizontally requires either sticky sessions so clients return to the same server, or externalizing state to a shared store. Sticky sessions reduce fault tolerance and create imbalance, while externalizing state removes those limits but adds complexity: you must design a durable, consistent store and handle cache invalidation, performance, and availability of that store. A common misconception is that moving state to a single shared database solves scaling automatically; it can create a new bottleneck if the store itself is not designed to scale or cache efficiently. The right architecture combines stateless application servers with distributed caches or databases tuned for scale. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Externalizing state means moving session data or other client-specific information out of application memory into a shared store. Common choices include an in-memory cache like Redis or a distributed database. The benefit is that application servers become stateless: they can be added or removed without losing sessions, and any server can process any request. These three concepts capture the most important ideas to keep in mind. First, Horizontal Scaling means adding machines to increase capacity and fault tolerance, but requires coordination around state and routing. Second, a Load Balancer distributes traffic, performs health checks, and provides a stable client endpoint while preserving headers that backends may need. Third, Round Robin, Least Connections, and IP Hash are common algorithms with clear use cases: Round Robin for uniform short requests, Least Connections for long-lived sessions or uneven load, and IP Hash when you need simple client affinity. Remember that selecting an algorithm is a trade-off, not a silver bullet. Use affinity only when necessary and prefer externalized state for true horizontal scalability. These three ideas will guide your decisions when designing systems that must scale reliably.

Here are three practical reminders to carry forward. First, prefer externalizing session or client state into a shared store like Redis before aggressively horizontal scaling; this makes app servers interchangeable. Second, configure health checks and header forwarding so backend visibility and fault handling are reliable; missing X-Forwarded-For or no health checks create operational blind spots. Third, when asked in interviews, explain why you would choose a specific algorithm: name the workload characteristic that motivated your choice, a concrete example like chat or token validation, and one mitigation for each downside. These concise practices will help you design and communicate scalable systems that handle growth while keeping operational complexity manageable.
